# Human-Centred LLM Privacy Audits: Findings and Frictions

**Authors:** Dimitri Staufer Affiliation: TU Berlin, Berlin, Germany email: staufer@tu-berlin.de , Kirsten Morehouse Affiliation: Columbia University, New York, USA email: km4252@columbia.edu , David Hartmann Affiliation: TU Berlin, Berlin, Germany Affiliation: Weizenbaum Institute for the Networked Society, Berlin, Germany email: d.hartmann@tu-berlin.de and Bettina Berendt Affiliation: TU Berlin, Berlin, Germany Affiliation: Weizenbaum Institute for the Networked Society, Berlin, Germany Affiliation: KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium email: berendt@tu-berlin.de

## Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) learn statistical associations from massive training corpora and user interactions, and deployed systems can surface or infer information about individuals. Yet people lack practical ways to inspect what a model associates with their name. We report interim findings from an ongoing study and introduce LMP2, a browser-based self-audit tool. In two user studies ( $N_{total}{=}458$ ), GPT-4o predicts 11 of 50 features for everyday people with $\geq$ 60% accuracy, and participants report wanting control over LLM-generated associations despite not considering all outputs privacy violations. To validate our probing method, we evaluate eight LLMs on public figures and non-existent names, observing clear separation between stable name-conditioned associations and model defaults. Our findings also contribute to exposing a broader generative AI evaluation crisis: when outputs are probabilistic, context-dependent, and user-mediated through elicitation, what model–individual associations even include is under-specified and operationalisation relies on crafting probes and metrics that are hard to validate or compare. To move towards reliable, actionable human-centred LLM privacy audits, we identify nine frictions that emerged in our study and offer recommendations for future work and the design of human-centred LLM privacy audits.

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly inform decisions in high-stakes domains and appear in everyday assistants for health, finance, and counselling tasks (Jung et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a). They are trained on massive, web-scraped corpora and shaped through user interactions that include sensitive information about individuals (Kuru, 2024; Ruschemeier, 2025; Nolte et al., 2025). Aggregated across domains, these data enable increasingly fine-grained indirect identification and profiling, turning LLM-based applications into systems that scale opaque personalisation and inferences about individuals. In doing so, they (a) violate contextual integrity (Nissenbaum, 2004) by repurposing data beyond the context in which it was shared (Barnes, 2006; Dienlin and Trepte, 2015), (b) create individual-level harms via misinference (Staab et al., 2024; Custers and Vrabec, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), exposure (Huang et al., 2022; Nasr et al., 2023), discrimination (Kadoma et al., 2025; Hartmann et al., 2025), and targeted persuasion (Krauß et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025; Alberts et al., 2024) and (c) produce societal harms by concentrating informational power (Kraft et al., 2025; Couldry and Mejias, 2019) while making accountability attribution opaque (Cobbe et al., 2023), normalizing surveillance (Windl et al., 2025; Schaub et al., 2016), and weakening autonomy and democratic agency (Tufekci, 2015). One direction to more transparency about these practices are self-audits. Organisational privacy audits review data practices, but they do not tell individuals what an LLM associates with their name or broader identity signals, such as language use or inferred demographic attributes (e.g., location, education, age) (Preoţiuc-Pietro et al., 2015; Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil et al., 2012; Staab et al., 2024). We therefore focus on human-centred self-audits that make these associations observable and contestable. In line with calls for human-centred evaluation (Liu et al., 2025), end-users and other impacted stakeholders should be able to assess model behaviour to adapt their interactions, provide feedback, and challenge harmful outputs.

In this HCI context, we define privacy self-auditing as a user-facing practice that lets individuals inspect what a system associates with their name (or their broader identity), interpret those associations, and decide on actions such as correcting or erasing them. Such a procedure presumes inspectable records. However, (1) LLM outputs are stochastic and sensitive to elicitation choices, (2) black-box APIs hide internals, and (3) prompt responses are weak evidence of system behaviour (Hase et al., 2023; Schlangen, 2021; Gehrmann et al., 2023; Nakka et al., 2024; Kiela et al., 2021). Commercial conversational agents offer application-level memory controls, but these govern explicit “memories” and do not reveal model-level name-conditioned or otherwise inferred associations. Users cannot inspect or control these associations, and they may influence downstream applications built on the model. They may involve sensitive traits (e.g., religion, sexual orientation, political affiliation, or health) that can be benign or affirming for one person and risky or unwanted for another, depending on the social, cultural, or legal context. Our focus is on probing such associations and presenting signals that users can interpret. We report interim findings and argue why human-centred LLM privacy audits remain challenging despite growing technical work on memorisation (Carlini et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022) and inference (Staab et al., 2024).

Our goal is twofold: (1) report findings about name-conditioned information on individuals in LLMs, and (2) articulate the methodological, legal, and UX challenges that make privacy self-auditing difficult in practice. We introduce LMP2 (Language Model Privacy Probe)11 1 https://anonymous.4open.science/r/human-centered-llm-privacy-audit-E05D, a self-audit tool that adapts canary probing to black-box APIs and presents user-facing association strength and confidence signals (Figure 1). This complements work on user-driven and external auditing, as well as audit tools that support these approaches by presenting clear, actionable evidence (DeVos et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2023; Lam et al., 2022; Metaxa et al., 2021; Ojewale et al., 2025; Hartmann et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025).

## 2. Audit Method and Tool (LMP2)

We operationalise self-auditing as a user-initiated audit in which name-conditioned associations are probed across prompt variants to surface stable signals about a property value, e.g., a person’s residence. Building on WikiMem (Staufer, 2025), we use canaries—short probe sentences that assert a subject–property–value triple $(h,p,v)$ , where $h$ is the name, $p$ the property, and $v$ the value—and select 50 human properties from WikiMem’s 243 Wikidata properties (including date of birth, occupation, and phone number). This subset reflects features with broad user relevance, coverage across categories (e.g., core identity, personal and professional life), and expressibility in one to three words. For each property we use up to five low-ambiguity paraphrases of the canaries. Because black-box APIs only expose probabilities over model-generated completions, we reformulate the probes as a fragmented sentence recovery task (Figure 2). We truncate user-provided ground truths to two-character prefixes, generate 20 random counterfactual prefixes, and instruct the model to output only the corrected last word(s).

We aggregate across paraphrases and counterfactuals to produce two user-facing metrics. Association strength combines how often a value is produced with its average probability (or vote weight when log-probabilities are unavailable), then normalises evidence across the top candidates. Confidence captures how concentrated that evidence is, indicating whether outputs converge on a single value or remain dispersed.

LMP2 implements this audit method as a browser--server tool that keeps user-entered values in the client22 2 User-entered ground-truth values are not retained beyond the session. However, the provider necessarily receives the submitted names and prefixes, to which participants explicitly consented., queues requests in the backend, and returns Results Cards with top predictions and confidence scores (Figure 1). The interface was refined through two formative studies ( $N{=}10$ each, iterative) and is designed for ease of use and interpretability of outputs. Users enter their full name and select features to probe. The backend converts user inputs into fragment-completion queries (two-character prefixes combined with paraphrased probes) and submits these to the model provider (Figure 3). Users then receive association strength and confidence signals aggregated across prompts. In our study, participants were then asked to provide feedback about the generated predictions (accuracy, privacy violation, feeling).

## 3. Findings from the Ongoing Study

### Empirical audit across eight LLMs.

We compare three open models (Qwen3 4B Instruct, Llama 3.1 8B, Ministral 8B Instruct) and five API-based models (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini Flash 2.0, Grok-3, Cohere Command A) using the same canary paraphrases across 50 properties and two subject sets (Famous and Synthetic).

*Figure 4. Distribution of confidence across models and subject sets: Confidence separates famous from synthetic individuals across models, indicating stable name-conditioned associations for users with high web presence.Density plots of confidence for Famous and Synthetic individuals across eight models. Famous distributions peak at higher confidence, while Synthetic distributions shift lower, with the clearest separation in Grok-3 and GPT-5.*

- • Subject-set separation. Confidence separates Famous ( $n{=}100$ public figures with extensive Wikipedia coverage and multiple ground truths) from Synthetic ( $n{=}100$ recombined, non-existent names), indicating stable name-conditioned associations for high web presence (Figure 4).

- • Property type effects. Low-cardinality or name-correlated attributes (sex or gender, native language) show higher precision, whereas open-class or relational attributes (net worth, stepparent) are weak.

- • Sensitive facts for public figures. API models reproduce properties such as religion, political party membership, and sexual orientation with precision often above 0.8.

- • High-confidence errors. Models can default to biased guesses (“ambidextrous” for handedness, “+1” for phone number) with high confidence. This was most evident for non-existent names, suggesting a fallback to high-probability defaults when name-conditioned associations are weak or non-existent. Ministral 8B Instruct was the only model that instead exhibited a near-uniform output distribution on the Synthetic set.

- • Model differences. Larger API models are significantly more accurate on Famous than smaller open-source ones (Grok-3 $f_{1}{=}0.54$ , GPT-5 $f_{1}{=}0.47$ vs. Ministral 8B Instruct $f_{1}{=}0.16$ , Qwen3 4B $f_{1}{=}0.19$ ).

### User studies with EU residents.

To explore whether name-conditioned associations also emerge for regular (non-famous) people, we ran one survey and two tool-based studies with adult EU residents33 3 In our ongoing study, we focus on EU residents because our legal discussion centres on the GDPR and associated data subject rights (e.g., access, rectification, and erasure), which apply within the EU. on Prolific.

- • Interest and concerns. In an initial survey ( $N{=}155$ ), 60% expressed interest in a self-audit tool. Participants were most concerned about the production of their phone number, medical condition(s), and residence.

- • Feature selection in tool use. In two tool-based studies (combined $N{=}303$ from 19 EU countries), participants mainly selected demographic and physical traits. Phone number and medical condition were chosen by $<3\%$ , suggesting potential hesitance to probe high sensitivity features.

- • Model performance. GPT-4o produced 11 of 50 features with $\geq$ 60% accuracy, including sex or gender (94.4%), sexual orientation (82.9%), native language (77.8%), eye colour (74.3%), and hair colour (74.1%). The average accuracy across all selected features was 45% (See Appendix, Table 2). Notably, accuracy remained high even for low-frequency traits (e.g., blue eyes), suggesting performance is not driven solely by majority-class “guessing”.

- • Perceptions and control. 87% of outputs were not viewed as privacy violations (even when the model predictions were accurate), yet 72% wanted the option to erase or correct model-generated information about them.

## 4. Frictions in Human-Centred LLM Privacy Auditing

### Auditing as socio-technical practice.

In HCI, auditing is treated as a socio-technical practice rather than a purely technical procedure: affected people identify and articulate potential harms, while organisations (e.g., platforms, regulators, or researchers) provide tools, procedures, and accountability pathways that support user sensemaking and investigation (Metaxa et al., 2021; DeVos et al., 2022; Lam et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2023). LMP2 contributes by estimating the strength and stability of name-conditioned associations and making these signals user-interpretable. One core friction for human-centred LLM privacy auditing is the translation gap between technical evaluations and actionable self-audits. Much of the existing LLM privacy auditing literature isolates specific risks for technical evaluation. For example, research focuses on (i) extractability (Carlini et al., 2019; Carlini et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022; Nasr et al., 2023; Nakka et al., 2024), (ii) memorisation (Panda et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2025; Staufer, 2025), (iii) attribute inference (Staab et al., 2024), (iv) demographic or representational harms (e.g., stereotyping and bias), or (v) interface-level controls (e.g., application “memory” settings). Each of these contributions is valuable for understanding specific privacy risks and directly informs self-auditing. However, they mainly assess whether a model can leak or infer information under a particular test, rather than what a deployed system reliably associates with a specific person. Moreover, without an explicit link between measurement and remedy (e.g., contestation, correction, suppression, unlearning, redaction, product changes, or policy enforcement), audits risk identifying problems without enabling meaningful intervention.

### Ambiguity around audit scope.

Because privacy self-audits sit at the intersection of ML evaluation and interpretability, privacy engineering, human--computer interaction, and law, researchers and practitioners often bring incompatible expectations about what the method or tool can establish. In our case, some readers (a) mistook model-level name associations with application-level memory controls, (b) treated probabilistic inferences about named individuals as non--privacy-relevant because they are not deterministic disclosures, (c) interpreted our prefix truncation strategy as a privacy-preserving measure (even though it is a pragmatic black-box adaptation for chat APIs44 4 Chat APIs only score their own completions—not arbitrary canary strings—so we framed it as a fragment-completion task around $(h,p,v)$ with two-character prefixes and aggregate evidence across paraphrased probes.), or (d) treated a correct output as proof of memorisation. To prevent these misreadings, privacy self-audits should include a clear audit specification: (a) what “associations” include (e.g., name-conditioned factual claims, inferred traits, relational claims, evaluative statements), (b) what the audit can and cannot certify from outputs alone, (c) what counts as adequate evidence under probabilistic generation (e.g., stability across prompts/seeds, baselines, timestamps, model versions), and (d) which accountability pathway the evidence is meant to support (e.g., user sensemaking, provider debugging, or legal contestation). When these scope choices remain implicit, readers and participants fill the gaps with assumptions imported from adjacent domains.

### Study context shapes what is observed.

Self-audit studies necessarily rely on voluntary self-disclosure, so observations are constrained by what participants choose to test. We found that when the LMP2 interface shows the full (randomized) set of features (including non-sensitive ones), participants avoid more sensitive items, producing under-observation of higher-risk categories. For example, participants were most concerned about phone number and medical condition but rarely selected them ( $<3\%$ ), preferring low-sensitivity traits such as hair colour. This mirrors challenges in user-engaged audits, where participation, incentives, and comfort levels shape what issues can be surfaced (DeVos et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2023; Lam et al., 2022).

### Memorisation, inference, and base-rate guessing are entangled.

Our results contribute to a growing literature documenting that LLMs can memorise training data (Carlini et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022) and infer traits from correlated cues (Staab et al., 2024). Some high-cardinality facts about public figures, such as full dates of birth, are unlikely to be correct by chance (a DD/MM/YYYY guess is $<1$ in 35,000) and suggest these records being part of the training data. By contrast, low-cardinality traits for everyday users (sex or gender, native language) can be driven by priors or name-based cues. In our user study, participants who believed their national or cultural background could be inferred from their name reported substantially higher prediction accuracy across features (50.3% vs. 28.4%). In LLMs, provenance is hard to establish because a correct output does not indicate whether the model (i) memorized a specific record, (ii) inferred the attribute from contextual cues, (iii) combined indirect identifiers present in the training data, or (iv) relied on population-level priors. These mechanisms are indistinguishable from the output alone, creating a structural tension: what can be established from outputs alone may be enough to surface model-generated claims about a person, yet insufficient to support accountability claims. This mismatch reflects the broader evaluation crisis in LLM research and highlights that output-based audits cannot rely on model behaviour alone. They require complementary sources of evidence. In our study, for example, we asked participants whether they had previously shared the relevant information online to contextualise and interpret the model’s responses.

### Indirect identification and name ambiguity.

Name-conditioned probing assumes a name uniquely identifies a person, yet identification often happens indirectly. Writing style, occupation cues, or location hints can lead models to attach attributes even when a name is common, extending audits beyond name-only measurements (Staab et al., 2024). Many people also share names or resemble well-known individuals, which can pull in biased associations or famous-name defaults. Disambiguating requires context (e.g., “Jane Doe from Stuttgart”), but more context can itself introduce bias or steer the model toward stereotypes (Eskandari Miandoab et al., 2025). Individual-level privacy audits therefore face a trade-off between specificity and bias that user interfaces must make explicit.

### Multiple ground truths and temporal drift.

Many personal attributes are multi-valued (e.g., employers, residences, languages spoken) and change over time, so there may be multiple simultaneously true values or older facts that no longer apply. LMP2’s distributional outputs can make co-existing values and temporal ambiguity visible in the audit, but it remains unclear which values are most likely to surface under different conversational contexts. More broadly, it is largely unclear how LLMs distinguish more recent from outdated facts (Wallat et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b), and factual belief updating remains an open problem (Hase et al., 2023). Critically, multiplicity does not reduce the harm of information surfacing tied to an identity because inaccurate or false inferences are problematic too when publicly attached to a person (European Data Protection Board, 2024; Nolte et al., 2025; Häuselmann and Custers, 2024). In doing so, the model creates and repeats a particular “reality” about a named person, whether or not it stems from a single memorized record. Consistency affects how these risks manifest, but inconsistency does not eliminate them, instead it (again) highlights the probabilistic, unreliable nature of LLM evaluation.

### Beyond normatively factual attributes.

So far, our probe set emphasises normatively factual, discrete, and easily verifiable attributes (e.g., eye color, date of birth). Yet privacy law and HCI research emphasise that personal data extends beyond such attributes to inferred profiles, contextual and relational data, and subjective or evaluative statements whose status and sensitivity vary by context and culture (Nissenbaum, 2004; Schomakers et al., 2021; Belen-Saglam et al., 2022; Ortlieb and Garner, 2016; Custers and Vrabec, 2024; Rupp and von Grafenstein, 2024; Häuselmann and Custers, 2024; European Data Protection Board, 2024). In this broader space, facts can be ambiguous or contested, and even nested evaluations like “Anna’s father was a good cook” blend relational information with reputational judgment, complicating what counts as personal data and what ground truth should be used for auditing.

### Language and script coverage.

Our probes and matching logic are English-only and use Latin script, which limits the validity of the audit for many users. Prior work documents that NLP research and evaluation are heavily skewed toward a small set of (often high-resource) languages, questioning language-agnostic behaviour (Joshi et al., 2020; Bender and Friedman, 2018). Moreover, what constitutes a “sensitive attribute” and what counts as harmful “bias” are context-dependent and normative, and may not transfer cleanly across linguistic and cultural settings (Blodgett et al., 2020; Selbst et al., 2019). Name cues are likewise socially interpreted and their perceived signals vary across countries and groups, making English/Latin-script proxies especially brittle (Ghekiere et al., 2025; Gautam et al., 2024). Finally, our observations about biased “guesses” for non-existent people would likely differ under non-Latin scripts because (a) this would itself provide an indirect identifier, and (b) tokenisation and representation quality vary substantially across languages and scripts in multilingual and commercial LLMs (Rust et al., 2021; Sindhujan et al., 2025).

### Deployed systems complicate evidence and actionability.

Deployed LLM applications increasingly use tool-augmented setups (e.g., web lookup, retrieval, agentic pipelines), which blend model behavior with shifting external sources (Borgeaud et al., 2022; Strauss et al., 2025). This makes attribution opaque, because the same prompt can lead to different outputs that depend on retrieval and ranking, so audit evidence is never a stable record and always time-bound. At the same time, subsequent legal and organisational steps often expect deterministic proof of what a system “knows” (Custers and Vrabec, 2024; Häuselmann and Custers, 2024; Rupp and von Grafenstein, 2024; European Data Protection Board, 2024). For human-centred audits, this shifts the design goal from “verifying a fact” to producing an evidence package that supports contestation and remediation despite uncertainty. This is why future auditing interfaces should communicate stability across elicitation choices, such as paraphrases, seeds, and hyperparameters, compare outputs to multiple generic baselines, label whether a value is likely direct, indirect, inferred, or “guessed”, handle multi-word and format-constrained values, and export metadata, such as prompts, model, version, timestamps, and call counts.

## 5. Conclusion

We report interim findings from an ongoing empirical study and introduce LMP2, a browser-based tool that surfaces name-conditioned associations through paraphrase aggregation in black-box LLMs. Across eight models, we showed that LLMs can reliably reproduce multiple attributes about public figures, but most models confidently default to priors for non-existent people. In user studies with EU residents, GPT-4o predicts 11 of 50 personal features with $\geq$ 60% accuracy, and participants overwhelmingly report wanting the ability to correct or erase model-generated associations.

Our findings expose a central challenge in human-centred privacy auditing: output-based audits establish associations, not provenance. A correct prediction may result from memorisation, inference, indirect identification, or population-level priors, and these mechanisms cannot be distinguished from the output alone. Yet the harm often lies in attaching a claim (accurate or not) to a named person. This distinction between association and provenance is essential for interpreting audit results and assessing their relevance under legal frameworks, such as the GDPR. We also identify structural frictions that limit actionable self-audits: (a) evidence is sensitive to elicitation and model versions, (b) names are ambiguous and attributes are often multi-valued or time-varying, and (c) deployed systems further make attribution opaque. These challenges situate privacy self-auditing within a broader generative AI evaluation crisis, where probabilistic, context-dependent outputs are in conflict with expectations of determinism and proof.

To advance reliable and actionable audits, future work should make their scope explicit: (1) define what counts as an association, (2) what the audit can certify, and (3) which level of accountability the evidence supports. Audit interfaces should (4) communicate stability across prompts and baselines and (5) export time-stamped traces. Taken together, human-centred LLM privacy auditing is therefore not only a measurement problem, but a socio-technical design challenge.

Who is American? A comprehensive analysis of the American = White/ Foreign = Asian stereotype (2007– 2023)

Kirsten N. Morehouse 1, Tessa E. S. Charlesworth 2, Thierry Devos 3 & Mahzarin R. Banaji 1

Against the backdrop of increasing ethnic diversity in the U.S., we replicate, extend, and challenge previous examinations of the American = White/Foreign = Asian stereotype in the largest sample to date (N = 666,623 respondents) over 17 years (2007–2023). Six key findings emerged. First, a robust American = White association emerged on implicit (Cohen’s d = 0.50) and explicit (Cohen’s d = 0.51) measures. Second, the strength of this effect varied by respondents’ race/ethnicity with implicit stereotypes strongest among White respondents (Cohen’s d = 0.86) and absent among East Asian respondents (Cohen’s d = 0.02). Third, the strength of implicit stereotypes was modulated by age, religion, and ideology—older, Christian, and conservative respondents displayed stronger implicit American = White associations—but not gender or education. Fourth, respondents living in U.S. metropolitan areas with greater Asian representation or a history of voting for Democratic candidates exhibited weaker implicit American = White associations. Fifth, over the past 17 years, implicit and explicit American = White associations decreased by 41% and 47%, respectively, and 14/14 demographic subgroups changed towards neutrality. Finally, we observed suggestive evidence that implicit stereotype trends towards neutrality were temporarily disrupted during the COVID-19 pandemic for White Americans but not Asian Americans.

Keywords  Ethnic-national stereotypes, Implicit/explicit stereotype change, Implicit Association Test, American = White association

In 1999, Wen Ho Lee, an American nuclear scientist working at the Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico, was accused of transferring American nuclear secrets to the Chinese government. Although indicted on 59 charges by a federal grand jury, a separate federal investigation failed to find support for the espionage charges. Ultimately, Lee received $1.6 million in damages from the government and media outlets, and an apology from the judge who had denied him bail.

The incident led Devos and Banaji1 to ask whether this case reflected a broader tendency to associate ‘American’ with some ethnic-national groups (e.g., European American) more than others (e.g., Asian American). Indeed, in convenience samples of college students, they discovered that European Americans were more strongly associated with the concept ‘American’ than Asian Americans on the Implicit Association Test (IAT;2). The existence of this American = European American/Foreign = Asian American stereotype (hereafter referred to as the American = White effect) was striking, given that previous research primarily documented implicit associations that were inherently subjective, such as implicit attitudes or preferences. Unlike a preference with no truth value (e.g., a preference for mountains over beaches), American–Foreign stereotypes can be evaluated against a factual basis: European Americans and Asian Americans are both members of the superordinate category “American.” Thus, while social and cultural features can intervene to shape which American groups are perceived as more American3,4, such biases contradict the fundamental principle that all citizens are equal citizens.

In a series of follow-up studies, Devos and colleagues used the IAT to investigate the nature of the American = White effect (for explorations using other measures, see4–7). This work led to three main findings.

First, they showed that the American = White effect was not restricted to White Americans respondents; in small community samples, Asian Americans also associated European Americans with ‘American’ and Asian Americans more with ‘Foreign’1. Second, the American = White effect persisted even when its factual inaccuracy was made conspicuous: White European celebrities of the time (e.g., Kate Winslet, Hugh Grant) were more strongly associated with “American” than were Asian American celebrities (e.g., Lucy Liu, Michael Chang;1,8). Third, this American = White effect emerged when White Americans were compared to other ethnic groups (e.g., Black Americans, Latinx Americans), pointing to its generality1,9–12. In fact, European Americans were more strongly associated with “American” than Native Americans, who are indigenous to North America11, challenging the idea that the American = White effect simply reflects the timeline of immigration to the United States.

Overview of the present research The present work provides a comprehensive investigation of the American = White association over the past 17  years (2007–2023). In doing so, it replicates, extends, and challenges previously reported results. This investigation is particularly timely, given the changing demographic landscape in the United States. In 1980, Asians constituted 1.5% of the U.S. population13; today, they represent 7%14. Even in the last two decades alone, the population of Asian Americans has nearly doubled, from 11.9 million in 2000 to 22.4 million in 202015. Moreover, the representation of Asians in media16 and politics17 has increased dramatically, further challenging the view that ‘American’ is synonymous with White. At the same time, events like the COVID-19 pandemic have highlighted the persistence and strength of the longstanding stereotype that Asian Americans are foreigners18–23.

Motivated by these societal changes and events, the present analysis leveraged data from over 660,000 tests across 17 years to provide the most comprehensive investigation of this stereotype to date. This investigation centered on three questions. First, what is the strength of the American = White effect? Specifically, we investigate (a) the overall strength of implicit and explicit American–Foreign stereotypes, with a focus on implicit stereotypes; and (b) the variability of stereotypes across respondent race/ethnicity. Second, what predicts variation in the American = White effect? Here, we probed variation both across respondent-level variables (e.g., race/ethnicity, political ideology) and across region-level features (e.g., ethnic diversity of a metropolitan area). Third, has the American = White effect changed over the past 17 years (2007–2023)? And if so, is change observed across all demographic groups (pointing to the role of macro-level variables like media) or only among certain groups (pointing to the role of demographic-specific ideologies)? Finally, we explored whether long-run stereotype trends were disrupted during or after the COVID-19 pandemic, supporting insights into how and for whom societal events can influence stereotypes.

Together, this work (a) replicates, extends, or challenges previous results; (b) resolves questions about whether and how the American = White effect has changed; and (c) provides empirical discoveries that can support the development of new hypotheses about the nature of ethnic-national stereotypes.

Results and discussion Strength of the implicit American = White effect among American respondents Overall implicit stereotype magnitude In the largest available sample to date, spanning a 17-year period, evidence of an implicit American = White effect was observed, IAT D = 0.24, t(509,910) = 358.94, p < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.50. That is, Asian Americans were more strongly associated with the concept of “Foreign,” and European Americans were more strongly associated with the concept of “American.”

Notably, this American = White effect emerged even though “Foreign” was represented entirely by non- Asian landmarks (e.g., Eiffel tower, Pyramid of Giza) in the IAT procedure. In fact, the inclusion of European landmarks such as the Eiffel tower and London Bridge, but not East Asian landmarks (e.g., Great Wall of China), provided a particularly conservative test of the American = White effect.

Implicit stereotype strength by respondent race/ethnicity Despite the overall strength of the effect, the degree of association varied substantially by respondents’ racial/ethnic membership. White American respondents displayed the strongest implicit American = White associations, with a large effect size: IAT D = 0.38, t(231,530) = 413.00, p < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.86. Third-party respondents (e.g., Black or Latinx respondents) similarly displayed an implicit American = White association, IAT D = 0.21, t(137,531) = 164.00, p < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.44, but to a lesser degree than White Americans (b = − 0.17, SE = 0.002, t(509,907) = − 109.63, p < 0.001). By contrast, East Asian American respondents displayed no American = White effect, IAT D = 0.01, t(98,543) = 7.23, p < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.02. Instead, they equally associated Asian and European Americans with the concepts of “American” and “Foreign.”

Finally, South Asians represent a unique group of interest. On the one hand, they are part of the category “Asian American,” and therefore may exhibit associations that align with East Asian respondents. On the other hand, the IAT included line drawings of Caucasian and East Asian faces. As such, South Asian respondents may exhibit associations that align with third-party respondents. Providing support for the latter hypothesis, South Asian Americans displayed a small American = White association, IAT D = 0.13, t(42,307) = 54.50, p < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.27, but to a lesser extent than White respondents (b = − 0.26, SE = 0.002, t(509,907) = − 105.53, p < 0.001) or third-party respondents (b = − 0.09, SE = 0.003, t(509,907) = − 33.23, p < 0.001).

Taken together, three findings are worth emphasizing. First, the magnitude of this overall American = White effect is striking; it was almost twice as strong as the effect of another non-factual stereotype, Human = White/ Animal = Black24. Second, unlike the samples of college students collected in the early 2000s, the East Asian respondents (n = 98,543) in the present data displayed no implicit American = White association. Third and

Strength of the explicit American = White effect among American respondents Strikingly, this American = White effect was similarly observed on a measure of explicit cognition. However, unlike data from the IAT, East Asian and South Asian respondents reported the strongest explicit American = White association and White and third-party respondents displayed the weakest explicit association (see Table 1; see SI Table 2.2 for post-hoc comparisons). That is, both East Asian (M = 0.74, t(98,543) = 209.00, p < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.67) and South Asian (M = 0.65, t(42,307) = 115.00, p < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.56) respondents were most likely to report that Americans of European descent are “more American” than Americans of Asian descent. In the General Discussion, we explore the possibility that this result reflects Asian respondents’ awareness of societal stereotypes, rather than their own endorsement of this belief. As noted above, White respondents (M = 0.38, t(231,530) = 228.00, p < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.47) and third-party respondents (M = 0.41, t(137,531) = 162.00, p < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.44) similarly endorsed this American = White association, but to a lesser extent than Asian respondents.

To summarize, although the overall effect size for implicit (Cohen’s d = 0.50) and explicit (Cohen’s d = 0.51) American = White effects was nearly identical, the degree of bias across racial/ethnic groups was reversed. Implicit stereotypes were strongest amongst White respondents whereas explicit stereotypes were strongest among Asian respondents.

The American = White effect is not reducible to pro-White attitudes Relative to “Foreign”, the term “American” is evaluated much more positively28. In fact, labeling groups as “Foreign” can engender negativity towards them28. This raises an important theoretical question: Are American = White associations merely an effect of attitude (liking) rather than a stereotype about national identity? In SI Appendix 5 we tested and eliminated the possibility that American = White associations are reducible to pro-White attitudes. Specifically, we conducted additional analyses and an experiment (N = 1500) to demonstrate that American = White associations are not driven by a valence matching between American and White (more positive), and Foreign and Asian (more negative).

Stereotype magnitude by respondent gender, religion, education, and political ideology Four of the six demographic variables emerged as significant predictors of overall implicit stereotype magnitude (2007–2023; see SI Appendix 3 for full regression output). Specifically, a significantly stronger implicit American = White association was observed among respondents who were older (vs. younger), more ideologically conservative (vs. ideologically liberal) and identified as Christian (vs. non-religious and vs. identifying with another religion). By contrast, respondents’ gender (men vs. women) and level of education (college-educated and non-college-educated) had little effect on IAT D scores (see Table 1). These patterns persisted when regression models controlled for covariation between demographic variables and when age, education, and ideology were represented with numeric, rather than categorical, values (see SI Appendix 3).

A slightly different pattern emerged for explicit stereotypes, with three demographic features emerging as significant predictors: race (as reported above), age, and political ideology. Mirroring implicit stereotypes, gender and education had little effect on stereotype magnitude and ideologically conservative (vs. ideologically liberal) respondents displayed stronger explicit American = White associations. However, diverging from implicit stereotypes, explicit stereotypes were consistent across religious subgroups and younger (vs. older) respondents displayed stronger explicit American = White associations (see Table 1). This latter pattern has been observed elsewhere11, but future work should explore whether it is driven by increased endorsement of the American = White association among young respondents, or a desire to signal stereotype awareness.

Stereotype magnitude by country of citizenship Given the content of this stereotype, the main analyses focus on data from American respondents (see SI Table 1.4). However, the present analyses harness data from over 70 countries to explore how nationality impacts the American = White effect (see also11,29).

Nationality did emerge as a significant predictor of implicit and explicit stereotypes (see Table 1; implicit: b = 0.10, SE = 0.0015, t(637,002) = 68.24, p < 0.0001; explicit: b = − 0.19, SE = 0.0064, t(637,002) = − 29.98, p < 0.0001). In particular, and consistent with the ingroup prototypicality effect29, a significant interaction between nationality and respondent race/ethnicity emerged. White respondents who were U.S. citizens displayed an implicit stereotype that was almost 70% higher than White respondents who were not U.S. citizens, b = 0.17, SE = 0.003, t(636,996) = 63.57, p < 0.0001. By contrast, East Asian respondents who were U.S. citizens displayed slightly weaker implicit American = White associations than East Asian respondents who were not U.S. citizens, b = − 0.04, SE = 0.003, t(636,996) = − 16.34, p < 0.0001. Similar results were obtained when using country of residence (rather than citizenship) to demarcate groups (see SI Appendix 4). Moreover, given that individual countries within East and South Asia vary in their culture and attitudes towards social groups30, country-level means are also reported in SI Appendix 4.

Predictors of stereotype variability: region-level features Even within the United States, significant variation was observed across geographic location. For example, average implicit stereotypes (across all time) ranged from 0.57 (Johnstown, PA) to 0.09 (San Francisco-Oakland- Fremont, CA; see SI Appendix 4 for MSA-level and state-level averages). Descriptively, this variation suggests that the strength of respondents’ American–Foreign stereotype may be tied to characteristics of their local environment. However, places vary along many interwoven features, such as demography (e.g., racial/ethnic composition) and structural features (e.g., local politics). In this section, we investigate the relationship between such regional features and stereotype strength. Specifically, focus on how the minority representation and the political ideology of a region may help explain variation in the implicit American = White effect (see SI Appendix 6 for explicit analyses).

Relationship between minority representation and implicit stereotype strength As observed in previous studies31, MSAs with larger percentages of East Asian residents (“minority representation”) displayed weaker implicit American = White associations, r = − 0.68 [− 0.744, − 0.600], t(220) = − 13.70, p < 0.001. Put differently, respondents living in areas with larger proportions of Asian residents had weaker implicit associations. To probe the robustness of this relationship, we additionally fit multilevel models that controlled for individual-level (i.e., respondent demographics) and region-level (i.e., median age, political leaning, total population) covariates. These models also included a random intercept for MSA to account for the nested structure of the data. Consistent with the correlation results, minority representation had a significant effect on implicit stereotypes, b = − 5.72, p < 0.001. Specifically, a 1 percentage point increase in minority representation predicted a 0.057 decrease in IAT D scores (see SI Appendix 4 for initial evidence that this relationship was modulated by respondents’ race/ethnicity).

In SI Appendices 4–5, we also report output from models exploring the relationship between implicit and explicit stereotypes and other regional features. For example, these models indicate that implicit stereotypes similarly decreased as a function of an MSA’s variety (the presence of multiple ethnic groups in an area31) and non-White population size but was far less responsive to the percentage of Black residents (see SI Table 4.13).

Relationship between regional ideology and stereotype strength Mirroring the finding that conservatives display stronger American = White associations than liberals, Republican and swing states have been shown to have stronger implicit American = White associations32. We replicated this pattern using a larger timespan (2007–2023), a more granular unit of analysis (MSAs rather than states), and a continuous measure of local ideology (percentage voting for a Republican presidential candidate). Specifically, increases in the percentage of the MSA voting for a Republican presidential or House of Representatives candidate corresponded to increases in the strength of the American = White association (|r > 0.35|; see SI Table 4.13). These patterns were replicated in multilevel models (b ≥ |2.3|; see SI Table  4.15).

Patterns of stereotype change Thus far, we have shown that while the magnitude of the American = White association varies by respondentlevel and region-level predictors, the stereotype is robust and prevalent across most demographic subgroups and geographic areas. Such bias prompted the following question: Can this strong and pervasive stereotype change or is it too deeply rooted? Previous research has documented that some implicit biases have shifted toward neutrality (e.g., sexuality and race bias) over the past decade while others have remained stable (e.g., disability and weight bias)33,34.

This question of change or stability in American–Foreign stereotypes was explored against the backdrop of a rapidly changing U.S. demographic landscape, with the population of Asian Americans growing faster than any other racial/ethnic group15. On the one hand, changes in demographics may translate into changing stereotypes, given that respondents living in areas with more minority representation displayed weaker American = White associations (see also31,35). On the other hand, the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the persistence of the perpetual foreigner stereotype, and the possibility that this stereotype has remained stable over the past 17 years. We examined these competing possibilities by exploring change overall and across demographic subgroups (see Analytic Strategy for details about time series analyses and SI Tables 4.1–2 for full ARIMA output).

Overall patterns of change (2007–2023) Over the past 17  years (2007–2023), both implicit and explicit stereotypes have moved towards neutrality. Crucially, implicit American = White associations decreased by 41% over the past 17 years, from a mean IAT D score of 0.35 in 2007 to 0.20 in 2023. ARIMA forecasts—which have been shown to reliably predict future change in implicit associations34—predict that implicit stereotypes could reach neutrality as early as 2035, should past trends continue. Even if implicit stereotypes take longer to reach neutrality than forecasted, the speed of change observed over the past 17 years is notable; a decrease of 41% makes American–Foreign stereotypes the second fastest changing implicit bias, measured over similar timeframes34. The only implicit bias that has recorded faster change is implicit sexuality bias (65% drop from 2007 to 2020).

Explicit American = Foreign associations changed toward neutrality at the same rate, decreasing by 47% from 0.67 in 2007 to 0.35 in 2023. Moreover, ARIMA forecasts project that explicit stereotypes could reach neutrality in just seven years, as early as 2030, should past trends continue.

Demographic differences in stereotype change Given this substantial change toward neutrality, we examined whether change was widespread across demographic subgroups or limited to particular demographic subgroups. Remarkably, for implicit stereotypes, 14/14 demographic subgroups recorded change toward neutrality over the past 17 years (see Fig. 1 for a visual depiction of subgroup trajectories and SI Table 4.1 for corresponding values). That is, despite change in overall stereotype magnitude, change was widespread. Indeed, respondents across self-reported gender, education, and religion not only showed shifts towards neutrality but changed in parallel (i.e., at the same rate). Even White and East Asian respondents, who displayed the largest gaps in stereotype strength, recorded similar levels of raw change (see Table 2).

Although every demographic group changed toward neutrality, two groups changed faster than others: selfidentified liberals and younger respondents showed a steeper reduction in implicit stereotypes than conservatives and older respondents, respectively. In fact, older respondents recorded the lowest rates of change of any demographic group (see Table 2). Supplemental analyses indicate that this pattern was driven by the Boomer generation, suggesting that early cultural experiences (e.g., small proportion of Asian Americans, proximity to wars fought in East Asia;36) may durably shape implicit stereotypes (see SI Appendix 6).

These widespread trends toward neutrality are promising, but it is worth emphasizing that only one demographic group has reached neutrality, i.e., to display no implicit American = White association. In 2016, East Asian Americans became the first and only group to reach neutrality. South Asian respondents are also projected to reach neutrality within the next year, should past trends continue. Nevertheless, all other groups displayed an American = White association, even at the most recent time point (see Table 2).

Change in explicit stereotypes was also observed in every demographic subgroup (see Fig. 1 and SI Table 4.2 for full ARIMA output with model parameters and forecasts). However, unlike implicit stereotypes, no group reached neutrality. In fact, ARIMA forecasts predict that it will take at least 12.4 years for East Asian respondents’ explicit stereotypes to reach neutrality if past trends continue.

Nevertheless, mirroring the results from implicit stereotypes, respondents’ explicit stereotypes changed towards neutrality in parallel, regardless of gender, education, or religion, and younger respondents changed more, in terms of raw change, than older respondents. Finally, diverging from implicit patterns, explicit stereotype trends converged for liberals and conservatives, with conservatives changing slightly more than liberals in terms of raw change (see Table 2).

Exploratory analyses of change during COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2023) We additionally sought to explore whether a major societal event—the COVID-19 pandemic—influenced longterm stereotype trends. Darling-Hammond and colleagues23 reported that implicit stereotype trends reversed course and began increasing in the three weeks following the proliferation of the term “Chinese virus” on Twitter (3/9/20–4/1/20). Other work similarly documented the consequences of such xenophobic language and actions18–22,37. With the benefit of more data covering the pandemic years, we explored whether the change observed in March 2020 was a reliable inflection point or only a temporary disruption (see34 for examples of temporary disruptions in attitude trends).

Trends across demographic subgroups. However, segmented regressions fit separately on data from White and East Asian Americans painted a more nuanced picture. These data indicated that the implicit stereotype trend reversal was driven by White Americans (see Fig. 2); no significant pandemic breakpoints were observed for East Asian Americans. By contrast, for explicit stereotypes, significant pandemic breakpoints were observed for both White and East Asian respondents, and at similar times.

Of course, these data alone do not permit causal claims and “what if” analyses suggest that these pandemic trends still fall within the 95% confidence intervals of predicted ranges (see SI Appendix 7). However, the results do appear to challenge previous findings that COVID-19 reversed implicit stereotype trends in March 202023, and can support future theorizing about how and when change might have occurred. For example, the uniformity in breakpoints for explicit but not implicit stereotypes is theoretically interesting. It suggests the sources of explicit stereotype disruption (e.g., media coverage) may have a more uniform effect across racial/ ethnic groups than the sources of implicit stereotype disruption, a hypothesis that can be tested in future work. Moreover, these data also highlight when COVID-19 may have influenced trends, supporting future tests about the cause of change, and hypotheses about the time-lag for societal events to impact stereotype trends.

General discussion Overall, the present paper provides the first comprehensive investigation of the American = White association. Although several of these findings have been reported in piecemeal fashion elsewhere, the current research offers three key contributions. First, it provides important benchmarking for the current strength of both implicit and explicit American–Foreign stereotypes in the largest sample to date (N = 666,623). Second, it examines individual, regional, and temporal features of this stereotype in a single location. Third, it charts patterns of change across the past 17 years (2007–2023), a period marked by substantial change for Asian Americans. Together, these findings elucidate new insights into the strength, patterns, and correlates of the cultural stereotypes of Asian Americans, thereby encouraging new empirically-derived hypotheses.

First, pointing to the magnitude of this stereotype, robust implicit and explicit American = European American/Foreign = Asian American (“American = White”) associations emerged in a massive sample of American respondents. In fact, the magnitude of the implicit stereotype reported here is likely a conservative estimate, given that “Foreign” was represented partially by European landmarks and the overrepresentation of East Asian and non-White respondents, who had markedly lower levels of stereotyping. Indeed, stereotype trends weighted to the US population indicate higher levels of bias (see SI Appendix 2). Thus, regardless of how the stereotype is assessed (on implicit or explicit measures) or analyzed (with or without weighting), we see clear evidence for a strong, but non-factual stereotype. Both groups have an equal probability of being American (p = 1), given that they are labeled as “Asian American” or “European American.” Yet, European Americans are consistently more associated with American (vs. Foreign) than Asian Americans.

Second, implicit and explicit American = White associations were observed in 13/14 and 14/14 demographic subgroups, respectively. However, although this stereotype was widely held, meaningful variations were observed in the degree of bias across respondent-level and region-level features. Most notably, East Asian and White respondents displayed opposite patterns of results. Specifically, East Asian respondents displayed no implicit American = White association, but the strongest levels of explicit American = White association. By contrast, White respondents displayed the strongest levels of implicit stereotyping, but significantly weaker explicit stereotypes than East and South Asian respondents. This dissociation amongst Asian American respondents may emerge because they routinely have their American identity questioned39, and therefore may be especially attuned to this perpetual foreigner stereotype. As such, Asian American respondents may (a) genuinely possess a feeling of being less “American” than their European counterparts; and/or (b) report that Europeans are more American because they are aware of this societal association, not because they endorse this stereotype.

In addition to variation across race/ethnicity, stronger implicit stereotypes were observed among Americans (vs. non-Americans), and American respondents who were older (vs. younger), more ideologically conservative (vs. ideologically liberal) and identified as Christian (vs. non-religious and vs. identifying with another religion). For explicit stereotypes, stronger stereotypes were observed among East Asian, younger, and conservative respondents. Ultimately, documenting these patterns across demographic groups is important as they can be used to create hypotheses about why American = White associations exist and potentially the types of interventions that can loosen their hold.

Interestingly, when aggregated to the region-level, indicators of both racial/ethnic composition and regional ideology continued to explain significant variation in stereotype strength. Specifically, building on previous work (e.g.,31), metropolitan areas with larger percentages of East Asian residents displayed weaker American = White associations. Similarly, MSAs with larger shares of residents voting for Republican candidates displayed stronger American = White associations. Future work should examine the mechanisms underlying this effect (e.g., contact driving the reduction of bias among MSAs with high minority representation) and the direction of this effect. That is, whether (a) local ideology impacts stereotype strength; or (b) the American = White effect is more consistent with conservative ideology, and therefore covaries with local ideology.

Third and finally, an analysis of change across 17 years (2007–2023) showed that the American = White effect is rapidly changing toward neutrality. Implicit stereotypes decreased by 41%, making American–Foreign stereotypes the second-fastest changing implicit bias. Explicit stereotypes similarly showed substantial decreases, with bias decreasing by 47%. Remarkably, implicit and explicit stereotypes moved towards neutrality in every demographic subgroup, pointing to the potential role of more societal-level factors in shaping long-term change. However, despite this widespread change, meaningful differences in the speed of change were observed. In particular, self-identified liberals and younger respondents showed a steeper reduction in implicit stereotypes than conservatives and older respondents, respectively. Indeed, further emphasizing the role of cultural experiences in both spurring or hindering change, respondents born between 1946 to 1964 (“Boomer” generation) displayed the lowest rates of change. These respondents were not only raised against the backdrop of WWII and the Korean

In addition to change overall and across demographic subgroups, we explored the potential role of COVID-19 in disrupting stereotype trajectories. We found that implicit stereotype trends were disrupted for White but not East Asian respondents, while explicit stereotypes were disrupted for both White and East Asian respondents, and at similar times. However, given the conservative pandemic range (2020–2023), future work should more clearly disentangle any effect of COVID-19 from other concurrent events (e.g., changes in media representation). In fact, with the current data in hand, future work is poised to explore questions including the lag (i.e., the delay between the event and stereotype change) or duration of the stereotype change following an event. Additionally, future work can consider differences in the lag and duration when the event is singular (e.g., a statement from a prominent individual) versus more diffuse (e.g., media information received during a long pandemic)34.

Overall, the present work provided a comprehensive investigation into the magnitude, predictors, and change of the American = White association in the largest sample to-date. At the highest level, results suggest cautious optimism. Implicit and explicit stereotypes reduced by 41% and 47%, respectively, and trends moved towards neutrality in every demographic subgroup. Moreover, demographic subgroup and region-level analyses point to predictors of where even more rapid change is observed and may help inform future interventions that decrease the American = White association more durably.

Materials and methods All original data collection reported in this manuscript was approved by Harvard University’s Institutional Review Board (identification code: IRB20-1024; date of approval: 6/8/2020) and conducted with informed consent and in accordance with relevant guidelines. All measures and materials are provided in the Supplementary Information (SI) Appendix 2, and reproducible cleaning and analysis scripts are publicly available from OSF: https://osf.io/7zg62/.

Respondents Volunteer respondents completed the Asian-European American IAT (also called the “Asian American IAT” or an “ethnic-national IAT”) on the Project Implicit demonstration website (https://implicit.harvard.edu) between January 1, 2007 and December 31, 2023. Project Implicit is a non-profit organization and international research collaborative that hosts internet-based IATs and other implicit measures. Respondents on the demonstration website can choose to complete one of several IATs and volunteer their time in exchange for learning more about their implicit associations. The database was retrieved from open data archived at the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/cpmfk/).

Following previous work with this data33,34,40,41, respondents who did not complete the measures of implicit and explicit stereotypes, or failed to meet the standards of the IAT D score algorithm42, were excluded from analyses. Additionally, because of the need to re-weight the data for demographic representativeness (see below) respondents without complete demographic information on age, gender, race, political ideology, education, and religion were excluded. Finally, given the content of this association, the primary analyses were restricted to respondents who resided in the United States and were US citizens (n = 509,991). That is, the findings reported in the main text rely on data from US respondents unless otherwise specified. Data from non-US citizens (n = 149,250) were retained for nationality contrasts (see “Stereotype Magnitude by Country of Citizenship”) and supplemental analyses (see SI Appendix 4). For detailed information about the data used in each section, see SI Table 1.4.

This final sample of respondents was female (63%) and liberal (54%), with a mean age of 28.4 (SDage = 12.67). Unlike many other tests on the demonstration site (e.g.,40), the present sample was majority non-White; specifically, it consisted of 45% White (n = 231,530), 19% East Asian (n = 98,543), 8% South Asian (n = 42,307), 8% Hispanic (n = 43,069), and 4% Black or African American (n = 20,975) respondents. Additional details about demographics are available in the SI Tables 1.1–1.3.

Materials Implicit stereotypes To measure the strength of implicit ethnic-national associations, respondents completed a standard 7-block Implicit Association Test (IAT;2). The target categories (European American, Asian American) were represented by line drawings of European and East Asian faces, and the attributes (American, Foreign) were represented by famous American landmarks (e.g., The White House, Hollywood sign) and foreign landmarks (e.g., Eiffel tower, Pyramid of Giza). None of the foreign landmarks were from Asia, creating a conservative test of the association between Asian with ‘Foreign.’ Images of stimuli are included in SI Appendix 2.

In this ethnic-national IAT, positive IAT D scores indicate a stronger association of European American (relative to Asian American) with the attribute American (over Foreign). Negative IAT D scores indicate a stronger association of Asian American (relative to European American) with the attribute American (over Foreign). For ease of reporting, we commonly referred to the categories European American and Asian American as “White” and “Asian,” respectively. Furthermore, in the context of this paper, “Asian” refers to individuals of East Asian descent. These broad labels are adopted because of the narrow context of the present study, but have inherent limitations25.

Explicit stereotypes To measure explicit stereotypes, respondents were asked to report their beliefs about the degree to which Americans of Asian or European descent are “more American” on a scale from − 1 (“I consider Americans of

Explicit attitudes To measure explicit attitudes, respondents reported their preference for Asian Americans or European Americans on a scale from 1 (“I strongly prefer Asian Americans to European Americans.”) to 7 (“I strongly prefer European Americans to Asian Americans.”), with the midpoint (4) representing equal liking for both groups (“I like European Americans and Asian Americans equally.”). Demographic variables Data about respondents’ age, gender, race/ethnicity, level of education, political ideology, religion, college major, occupation and geographic information (including their country or region of primary citizenship, their country or region of primary residence, their current zip code, and the zip code corresponding to their longest residence) were requested. To protect respondents’ privacy43, zip code data was aggregated into metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs).

Analytic strategy to measure differences across demographic groups Descriptive Statistics. For every demographic subgroup, mean levels of implicit and explicit stereotypes, one-sample t-tests, and corresponding Cohen’s d effect sizes were provided (see, for example, Table 1). These descriptive statistics were provided as an estimate of stereotype strength within each subgroup. For comparisons of stereotype strength across subgroups, see “Inferential Statistics.”

Inferential Statistics. A series of regression models were fitted to estimate demographic differences in stereotype strength. Specifically, linear regression models with IAT D score as the outcome variable and the demographic variable of interest (e.g., respondents’ race/ethnicity) were used to assess the main effect of the demographic variables on implicit stereotypes. Pairwise comparisons were used to assess whether demographic subgroups were significantly different from each other. Moreover, to control for covariation between demographic variables, we fitted additional models with all demographic predictors entered into the same model. We employed a similar analytic approach to estimate main effects of demographic variables on explicit stereotypes, conduct pairwise comparisons, and control for covariates. The only difference was that we fitted a series of robust regressions, rather than linear regressions, given that explicit stereotypes were measured on a 7-point Likert scale.

Analytic strategy to measure stereotype change Following Charlesworth and Banaji33, we use Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) timeseries models44 to assess stability or change of American–Foreign stereotypes. Briefly, these models (a) account for temporal autocorrelations; (b) capture non-linearity and seasonality in trends; and (c) offer intuitive forecasts about likely patterns of future change. Indeed, recently, Charlesworth and Banaji34 demonstrated that ARIMA forecasts for implicit and explicit attitude trends (based on data from 2007 to 2016) provided generally accurate estimates of more recent trends (from 2016 to 2020), thus placing further confidence in the validity of the ARIMA method.

Additionally, raking and weighting was used to ensure that any observed long-term changes were not attributable to changes in sample characteristics (e.g., sample becoming more liberal over time). These approaches adjusted the final monthly mean estimates to maintain similar demographic compositions over time (e.g., to ensure that the relative weight given to liberals vs. conservatives was similar over all time; see1,2 for details). Moreover, additional robustness analyses were conducted to ensure that the observed patterns of change were not a consequence of the weighting approach, repeat test-takers, or sample source (see SI Appendix for full details).

# Rethinking LLM Bias Probing Using Lessons from the Social Sciences

## Abstract

The proliferation of LLM bias probes introduces three significant challenges: (1) we lack principled criteria for choosing appropriate probes, (2) we lack a system for reconciling conflicting results across probes, and (3) we lack formal frameworks for reasoning about when (and why) probe results will generalize to real user behavior. We address these challenges by systematizing LLM social bias probing using actionable insights from social sciences. We then introduce EcoLevels – a framework that helps (a) determine appropriate bias probes, (b) reconcile conflicting findings across probes, and (c) generate predictions about bias generalization. Overall, we ground our analysis in social science research because many LLM probes are direct applications of human probes, and these fields have faced similar challenges when studying social bias in humans. Based on our work, we suggest how the next generation of LLM bias probing can (and should) benefit from decades of social science research.

## 1 Introduction

The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into nearly every domain of life has brought renewed scrutiny to the biases in these models. A growing body of works has shown that biases in LLMs often mirror systemic inequities in the human-generated data on which they are trained, and therefore can amplify existing inequalities (e.g., by perpetuating unfair outcomes; for a review, see Gallegos et al., 2024). In response, numerous probes (and mitigations) for LLM biases have been proposed. While many of these probes are direct applications of methods used to study bias in humans, connections between LLM bias probing and psychological theory are limited. In this work, we argue that the expanding number of bias probes introduces significant challenges for the field. We highlight these challenges and propose actionable changes to research practices that are grounded in insights from the social sciences. With increasing attention on the capabilities and limitations of LLMs, we believe the field is in a unique position to shape how social biases in LLMs are detected, discussed, and addressed, and that doing so systematically will magnify the impact of this research area.

As an illustrative example, suppose you are a Machine Learning (ML) researcher studying gender-occupation bias in a recently deployed LLM. The task of creating and evaluating job materials is an increasingly popular and consequential use case, so you decide to examine whether LLMs might impact gender hiring disparities. You identify dozens of probes that target gender bias (e.g., via sentence completion, coreference resolution, or template-based tasks) and eventually find two highly relevant papers. The first paper observes strong evidence of gender-occupation bias: LLMs consistently pair male-gendered names with historically male-dominated professions (e.g., surgeon-John) and female-gendered names with female-dominated professions (e.g., nurse-Emily; Morehouse et al., 2024; Exp. 1). The second paper observes minimal evidence of gender-occupation bias: the LLM assigns equivalent scores to resumes “authored” by male and female candidates when resume quality is comparable (Armstrong et al., 2024, Fig. 3).

This example highlights three main challenges introduced by the expanding number of bias probes: (1) determining which probe(s) to adopt, (2) reconciling conflicting results across probes, and (3) establishing whether obtained results will generalize to real user behavior. Addressing these challenges is both practically and theoretically important.

From a practical perspective, a structured approach for probe selection is needed for two reasons. First, choosing an inappropriate probe may hinder researchers’ ability to capture the intended construct (i.e., latent concept under investigation; see Fig. 1 and Table 1 for examples). Indeed, the predictive validity of a probe increases when the probe and target construct are equally general or specific – a phenomenon known as the correspondence principle (Ajzen & Fishbein, 1977). For example, Kurdi et al. (2021) examined the predictors of responses to a workplace hair discrimination case (construct: bias towards Black hair). Participants’ implicit attitudes toward Afrocentric hair texture were stronger predictors than general anti-Black attitudes (i.e., global feelings of positivity/negativity). Second, probes targeting similar constructs may not produce similar results (e.g., embedding-based tasks do not correlate with downstream tasks; Goldfarb-Tarrant et al., 2021; Delobelle et al., 2022), in part due to subjective decisions in probe design (e.g., Delobelle et al., 2022) and experiment configurations (Cao et al., 2022). Thus, decisions about probe selection can impact the presence and degree of observed bias.
